title: Tree-structured indexing
lead: ISAM, B+ tree invariants, search, insertion, deletion and variable-length entries.

sections.title: Multilevel indexes and ISAM
sections.html:
Why a multilevel index beats binary file search

A sorted Customer file supports zipcode BETWEEN 8800 AND 8999 by locating the first qualifying record then scanning right. Binary search repeatedly jumps to distant file positions and has fan-out 2.

Instead, store sparse routing keys and page pointers in a smaller file, then index that file recursively until its top fits one root page. A page can hold many pointers, increasing fan-out and reducing random page probes. ISAM fixes this routing hierarchy; B+ trees update it as data grows.

PDF pp. 1–5

ISAM routing and all source updates

root [40]
left internal [20,33] -> [10,15] [20,27] [33,37]
right internal [51,63] -> [40,46] [51,55] [63,97]
insert23 -> overflow of [20,27]
insert48,41,42 -> overflow chain of [40,46]
delete42 -> remove that overflow entry
delete97 -> leaf [63]
delete51 -> leaf [55]; internal separator51 remains

For separators K₁…Kₘ, child 0 handles k<K₁, child i handles Kᵢ≤k<Kᵢ₊₁ and the last handles k≥Kₘ. Insertions/deletions modify leaf/overflow pages, not the fixed non-leaf hierarchy. Overflow entries need not remain globally sorted.

PDF pp. 6–10

ISAM cost and its limit

If each index node has fan-out F, descending s levels reduces N candidate pages to N/Fˢ. Setting that to one gives s≈logFN. This counts routing depth; overflow-chain reads are additional.

Static upper levels simplify concurrent access because inserts do not restructure them. Heavy updates can create long overflow chains and destroy good lookup cost despite a shallow routing tree. Leaving initial free space delays this degradation; relatively static data is the favourable case.

PDF pp. 11–12

sections.title: B+ tree structure and lookup
sections.html:
B+ occupancy and source searches

d=2; initial root [13,17,24,30]
leaves: [2,3,5,7] <-> [14,16] <-> [19,20,22]
        <-> [24,27,29] <-> [33,34,38,39]
lookup5 -> first leaf -> present
lookup15 -> [14,16] -> absent
range k>=24 -> last two leaves

Every leaf has equal depth. In this convention non-root nodes hold d…2d entries and an internal node with m keys has m+1 children. Root occupancy is exceptional. Leaf links support scans despite noncontiguous allocation; internal nodes contain routing separators, while leaves contain the actual data entries.

PDF pp. 13–15

Fan-out and cached upper levels

The source uses d≈100 and 67% fill to estimate fan-out near 133. Powers of 133 explain how a shallow tree addresses millions of entries. At 8 KB/page, one root is 8 KB, 133 second-level pages roughly 1 MB and 17,689 pages roughly 138 MB.

These capacity calculations are approximate and depend on whether height counts routing levels or the leaf level, and on actual entry sizes. Cached upper levels remove some physical reads; tree height and I/O count are therefore not always identical.

PDF p. 16

sections.title: Insertion and splitting
sections.html:
Insert 8: leaf copy-up and internal push-up

insert8 into [2,3,5,7] -> [2,3,5,7,8] (overflow)
leaf split: [2,3] | [5,7,8]; copy separator5 to parent
parent becomes [5,13,17,24,30] (overflow)
internal split: [5,13] | [24,30]; push separator17 up
new root [17]
left internal children: [2,3] [5,7,8] [14,16]
right internal children: [19,20,22] [24,27,29] [33,34,38,39]

5 stays in a leaf because it is a data entry. 17 leaves the split internal node because its parent now separates those two child groups. Keys and child pointers move together. Creating a new root increases height by one while all leaves remain at the same depth.

PDF pp. 17–19

Insert 6 using redistribution

This figure starts again from the original root, not from the post-8 tree. Inserting 6 into [2,3,5,7] overflows it. Move 7 to the right sibling [14,16], producing [2,3,5,6] and [7,14,16]; change their parent separator from 13 to 7.

The sibling must share the relevant parent and have space. Redistribution avoids adding a page but accesses the sibling and updates the routing boundary. Treating this figure as the next step after insertion 8 would give the wrong state.

PDF p. 20

sections.title: Deletion, occupancy and key compression
sections.html:
Delete 19 and 20: leaf borrowing

Deletion finds and removes the entry. If a non-root leaf has at least d entries, no occupancy repair is needed. Otherwise try borrowing from an adjacent sibling with the same parent and more than d entries.

The source leaf [19,20,22] becomes [20,22] after deleting 19, which meets d=2. Deleting 20 leaves [22]. Borrow 24 from [24,27,29], yielding [22,24] and [27,29]. The parent separator becomes 27, the new right-leaf lower boundary. Borrowing changes the separator but does not remove a child pointer.

PDF pp. 21–22

Delete 24: leaf merge and root contraction

[22,24] - 24 -> [22]
sibling [27,29] has only d entries -> cannot lend
merge leaves -> [22,27,29]; delete parent separator27
right internal [27,30] -> [30] (underflow)
left internal [5,13] is at minimum
merge internals, pulling root separator17 down
new root [5,13,17,30]; remove empty old root

A leaf merge concatenates data entries and fixes leaf links. An internal merge also needs the parent separator between the two key/pointer groups. Underflow can propagate upward; removing an empty root decreases height without unbalancing leaf depth.

PDF pp. 23–24

Internal rotation and relaxed deletion

Page 25 explicitly uses a different left subtree. Its root separator is 22; left internal [5,13,17,20] can lend, while right internal [30] is underfull. Move separator 22 down into the right node and move left’s last child pointer with it; promote 20 to the root. The repaired nodes are [5,13,17] and [22,30], under root [20].

This rotation is not copying a leaf key. Practical implementations may relax half-full occupancy and remove only empty pages, trading space for fewer structural changes. Height then reflects the tree’s growth history rather than only its current tuple count.

PDF pp. 25–26

Variable-length entries and separator compression

For variable keys or (key,RID-list) entries, a count-based order d no longer predicts space. Occupancy should be measured in bytes; internal pages and leaves can then hold different numbers of entries.

The source keys robbed,robbing,robot share prefix rob, allowing suffixes bed,bing,ot plus one saved prefix. Internal separators need only enough key bytes to route correctly; suffix truncation removes unnecessary trailing bytes while preserving comparison boundaries. Tree structure, compression and collation must agree. ISAM suits static data; B+ trees accommodate dynamic updates and ordered scans.

PDF pp. 27–30

quiz.question: When the leaf [4,9,12,15,18] splits into [4,9] and [12,15,18], what happens to separator 12?
options: It is removed from every leaf
It is copied into the parent and retained in the right leaf
It is retained only in the left leaf
quiz.explanation: The right leaf starts at 12, so its parent boundary is 12. Copy that boundary into the parent but retain the data entry in the right leaf: a leaf-chain scan must still return 12. Internal-node splitting instead moves a separator up while preserving the leaf data.
